verses.1: Al-Mizan identifies al-Wāqiʿa, literally an adjective for an occurring event, as the Resurrection used like a proper name because it is so well known; it is therefore one of the Qurʾan’s names for that event. The conditional wording omits its consequent to magnify the Resurrection, though the chapter supplies its import: the faithful will triumph and the faithless lose. It takes kādhiba as an infinitive, so that its occurrence cannot be denied; the alternative makes it an adjective meaning that its occurrence is not false. Khāfiḍa and rāfiʿa together depict an overturning of the material cosmic order: hidden realities will be disclosed, the familiar causal order will vanish, mighty disbelievers and sinners will be abased, and the Godwary made mighty.

verses.4: Al-Mizan explains rajj as intense movement: rajjan, used as an unqualified absolute object, intensifies the quake of the whole earth beyond description, and the clause is either an apposition to or explanation of the Imminent Event. Bass means the mountains’ being ground into fine dust, though it may mean their being set in motion; habāʾ is dust or sunlit motes, and inbithāth dispersion. Azwāj means classes or categories, not spouses, so all humankind will become three groups.

verses.8: Al-Mizan takes aṣḥāb al-maymana as the people of felicity and success, from yumn, in contrast to aṣḥāb al-mashʾama, the people of misery. It rejects the interpretation of maymana as the right hand: its contrast is mashʾama, which means ill fortune rather than the left hand; had hands been intended, the counterpart would have been aṣḥāb al-shimāl. The rhetorical repetition magnifies their rank.
verses.9: Al-Mizan derives mashʾama from shuʾum and reads maymana and mashʾama respectively as felicity and misery.
verses.10: Al-Mizan reads the first ‘Foremost Ones’ as those foremost in good works and the second as their precedence in receiving God’s forgiveness and mercy. It treats the first two reported readings—hastening to all that God calls to and being first in faith and obedience—as returning to this meaning. Readings that identify prophets or particular believers, including the believer from Pharaoh’s people, Ḥabīb Najjār, and ʿAlī, are exemplars (tamthīl); the remaining proposals are weak unless likewise understood as exemplary characteristics. The grammatical analyses that make the second phrase either a predicate or emphatic repetition do not displace this exegetical conclusion.
verses.11: Al-Mizan presents verses 11–56 as the detailed destinies of the Foremost, the People of the Right Hand, and the People of the Left Hand. ‘Those brought near’ is best read as an independent statement about the Foremost rather than a predicate displaced by ‘in gardens of bliss.’ Nearness first applies spatially and then to non-spatial realities; God’s nearness signifies His encompassing all things, while a servant’s taqarrub is acquired through righteous deeds. The servant thereby reaches divine mercy and freedom from misery, and God grants a special degree of grace, mercy, and forgiveness. The muqarrabūn are thus the highest rank of the felicitous: the apex of ʿubūdiyya, attained when one’s will and deeds entirely conform to the Master’s will. This is divine allegiance, wilāya, and its people are God’s awliyāʾ; naʿīm and jannat al-naʿīm accordingly denote divine allegiance and its paradise. The plural gardens most likely gives each of them a garden, though a collective reading is possible. Al-Mizan takes the ‘former’ as earlier prophetic nations and the ‘latter’ as this community, so the brought-near are many from the former and few from the latter, rejecting a division internal to the Prophet’s community. Their brocaded, face-to-face reclining expresses unalloyed friendship, sincerity, and freedom from reproach or backbiting. Immortal serving youths continually attend them; the commentary prefers their eternal youthful state, while reporting an alternative derivation involving earrings. They bring vessels of visibly poured wine that causes neither headache nor loss of reason, together with whatever fruit and fowl are desired. Reports that fruit branches bend down and desired fowl arrive prepared and revive afterwards do not conflict with service at an assembly: Paradise gives them whatever they desire by either means. The big-eyed houris are women of Paradise, likened to guarded pearls for untouched purity, and all these gifts are recompense for the believers’ continuous righteous works. Paradise contains neither laghw, purposeless speech, nor taʾthīm, imputing sin; its recurrent speech is ‘Peace,’ though taʾthīm is also read as lying and the exception may be understood as sound speech. The People of the Right Hand are the earlier People of Good Fortune, now named for receiving their records in their right hands; the question about them is rhetorical admiration. Their setting includes thornless lote trees, fruit-laden clustered banana trees, unbroken shade, ceaseless water, and fruit available without season, inner distaste, fullness, distance, or other obstacle. Furush marfūʿa may mean elevated women rather than literal carpets, fitting the following description: they are specially created, remain unchanged by age and time, remain virgins despite intercourse, and are loving and of like age to their spouses. This group includes many believers from both earlier nations and the Prophet’s nation, unlike the brought-near, whose latter contingent is fewer. The People of the Left Hand are the People of Ill Fortune and receive their records in the left hand; the question about them conveys horror. Their punishment is penetrating infernal heat (samūm), boiling water (ḥamīm), and thick black smoke (yaḥmūm), whose shadow, unlike an ordinary shadow, is neither cool nor beneficial. Their worldly mutrafīn state was not merely material wealth but absorption in God-given comforts until they became proud and disobedient. Their persistent ‘great sin’ is, contextually, arrogant refusal of servanthood: they violated the fiṭra and the mīthāq pledged in ʿālam al-dharr by obeying other than God, the summit of shirk. The commentary records alternate explanations as idolatry, major sins generally, or oaths denying resurrection. They deemed resurrection, especially of their ancestors, improbable; the Prophet is commanded to answer that all former and latter generations will be gathered at a mīqāt, an appointed day known to God, with no real difference between their resurrection and their forefathers’. The astray deniers, whose obstinate denial has become a settled trait, will eat Zaqqūm, then drink boiling water without quenching like thirsty camels or parched ground. This food and drink is their nuzul on the Day of Recompense, a deliberately mocking ‘hospitality’ addressed by God to the Prophet rather than the conclusion of his speech to them.

verses.15: Al-Mizan says the brought-near recline on brocaded couches face to face (mutaqābilīn), an image of friendship, sincerity, and camaraderie without turning away, reproach, or backbiting.

verses.17: Al-Mizan explains that wildān mukhalladūn are eternally youthful serving boys who continually attend the brought-near; it reports, but does not prefer, a derivation of mukhalladūn from ‘earring.’ They carry akwāb without handle or spout, abārīq with a spout, and full kaʾs cups of visibly poured maʿīn wine, which causes neither headache nor stupefaction. They also serve whichever fruits and fowl the inhabitants desire. Reported fruit that bends down and fowl that arrive prepared, then revive after being eaten, do not conflict with such service, since Paradise provides whatever is desired both through attendants at gatherings and directly. The implicit clause gives these people big-eyed houris, the women of Paradise, whose guarded-pearl likeness denotes untouched purity. All this is recompense for their continuous righteous deeds.

verses.25: Al-Mizan defines laghw as speech without benefit or effect and taʾthīm as imputing sin, so Paradise contains neither idle talk nor accusations, since there is no sin there; taʾthīm may also mean lying. Its repeated speech is ‘Peace!’—not an exception that counts as sinful or vain, but an indication of frequent peace; the Arabic may also mean ‘except sound speech.’

verses.27: Al-Mizan identifies the People of the Right Hand with the earlier People of Good Fortune: they receive their records in the right hand. The rhetorical question turns to their fate while magnifying and expressing amazement at their state.
verses.28: Al-Mizan understands ‘clustered spathes’ as banana trees laden from top to bottom, while recording alternatives of any cool moist-shaded tree or an acacia; the clustering is their stacked fruit. Their Paradise also has shade undiminished by sun, continuously flowing water, and fruit neither seasonal nor prevented by internal distaste or fullness, or by external distance, thorns, or other barriers. Furush literally means carpets, but may denote women elevated in intelligence, beauty, and perfection, which fits the subsequent special creation.

verses.45: Al-Mizan explains that the People of the Left Hand are punished because worldly blessings made them mutrafīn: proud, disobedient, and preoccupied with comforts until they forgot everything else. This is not restricted to material wealth, since every person is surrounded by divine blessings and may be distracted from remembrance by the comfort they provide. Their persistence (yuṣirrūn) in the great sin is, contextually, their arrogant refusal of God’s servanthood. They violated the oath of their fiṭra and their mīthāq in ʿālam al-dharr by obeying other than God, the height of shirk. The commentary records alternatives that take ḥinth as itself ‘great sin,’ hence idolatry, as major sins generally, or as their oaths to deny the Resurrection.

verses.51: Al-Mizan treats this as the continuation of the Prophet’s warning about the Resurrection: astray deniers will eat Zaqqūm and fill their bellies with it. ‘Astray deniers’ identifies the settled traits that make them people of loss—their departure from truth, continuous obstinate rejection, and persistence in sin; mere error without denial could still admit guidance and salvation. It explains min in min Zaqqūm as either specifying the tree’s kind or appositional, and says the feminine pronoun may refer to the tree or fruit; the later masculine pronoun remains possible because both shajar and thamar take either gender.

verses.54: Al-Mizan reads ‘on top of it’ as drinking ḥamīm immediately after Zaqqūm. Hīm may be camels afflicted with huyām, an unquenchable thirst that makes them drink until death or grave illness, or parched ground that never fills; thus they drink the burning water without relief. This concludes the Prophet’s instructed warning to the idolaters.

verses.56: Al-Mizan says this is the food and drink offered to the astray deniers on the Day of Recompense. Calling that punishment nuzul, ‘hospitality,’ is mockery, and the address is God’s to the Prophet; if it continued the Prophet’s speech to them, it would say ‘your hospitality.’
verses.57: Al-Mizan reads ‘We created you’ as a rebuke to people who deny Resurrection and recompense. First creation proves that God can create them again; moreover, as their Creator and governor, He knows what He made, what will become of them, and His own purpose for them. They therefore have no excuse to reject the scriptural news that He will resurrect and recompense them for good and evil. The shift from third-person description to direct address sharpens the condemnation.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains tumnūn as emitting or discharging semen into women’s wombs.
verses.59: Al-Mizan takes the question to ask whether humans transform emitted semen into human beings or God does.
verses.60: Al-Mizan holds that creation is the outpouring of existence (ifāḍat al-wujūd), so every feature of finite human life, including death, proceeds from the Creator’s determination. Death is not an unintended consequence, a divine deficiency, or an external force that overpowers a God who meant humans to live forever; such a view would make His will constrained by the causal system He created. God deliberately ordained life followed by death, and is not outmaneuvered by it. He ordained death so generations replace one another and humans are recreated in a hitherto unknown, otherworldly creation; death is transition between abodes and kinds of creation, not annihilation. Amthāl means human beings of the same species, not merely changed bodily forms. The proposed reading mathal, by which people might be remade in animal forms, is judged less comprehensive and insightful.

verses.62: Al-Mizan argues that knowledge of the first genesis supplies the premises for accepting an everlasting Hereafter and recompense. The ordered world is neither blind nor purposeless; each species is guided to its proper felicity, and human guidance requires prophets, moral commands, and recompense for good and evil, which is not completed here. Since God created this world from nothing, its creation proves a second creation possible and refutes calling Resurrection absurd. It also supports bodily resurrection: a body enlivened in the Hereafter is like an earthly body, and like things share possibility of existence. The commentary rejects al-Zamakhsharī’s and al-Alūsī’s attempt to derive juristic qiyās or a fortiori analogy. This is qiyās burhānī manṭiqī, yielding certainty from likeness, not speculative ẓann; the Hereafter is not easier because pre-existing materials still depend wholly on God, nor does it follow an earlier ‘pattern,’ which confuses mithl, likeness, with mithāl, pattern. Although the resurrected body differs from the earthly one, the person remains the same because individual identity resides in the enduring spirit, not the constantly changing body, like Zayd in youth and old age.
verses.63: Al-Mizan says the questions about sowing, water, and fire demonstrate God’s rubūbiyya, His governance of the material world on which people depend. Taḥruthūn means ploughing and scattering seed; humans do not bring seed to maturity, whereas God can reduce the crop to dry fragments, leaving them stunned at their lost wealth, labour, and provisions. Natural causes genuinely contribute to growth, but neither they nor their own causes exist or operate independently of God; the whole causal chain is dependent on Him and manifests His blessings.

verses.68: Al-Mizan says God’s power to bring down drinkable water and make it bitter calls for shukr: beautiful remembrance of God and His blessings by manifesting servanthood in word and deed.

verses.71: Al-Mizan, citing al-Ṭabrisī, explains tūrūn through īrāʾ, kindling fire by striking flint, and muqwīn as desert-dwellers, from qiwāʾ, an empty place abandoned by its inhabitants. The verses ask whether humans caused the fire’s tree to grow, though God made the fire a reminder and a boon for those desert-dwellers.

verses.74: Al-Mizan says that after displaying divine lordship in creation, governance, resurrection, and recompense, God turns from obstinate idolaters to command the Prophet to glorify Him above their idolatry and denials. Fa makes this glorification follow that exposition, while bi may mean glorifying by uttering God’s Name, remembering God through the Name, or have the Name as the verb’s direct object; glorifying the Name then glorifies God Himself. Al-ʿAẓīm may qualify either the Name or the Lord.
verses.75: Al-Mizan treats ‘I swear not’ as an oath formula, though lā may be superfluous or a negation before the oath. It prefers mawāqiʿ al-nujūm as the places of stars in heaven, while recording readings of the term as stars’ falling on the Resurrection, shooting stars striking devils, or their western setting places.
verses.76: Al-Mizan says the verse magnifies and re-emphasizes the oath’s importance.
verses.77: Al-Mizan explains that denial of monotheism and Resurrection led the idolaters to deny the Qurʾan that teaches them; after adducing cosmic signs of those truths, the oath confirms the Qurʾan’s divine reality. Its unqualified description as karīm means that it is precious to God, praiseworthy, and supremely beneficial to humankind because it contains the realities needed for happiness in both worlds. ‘In a guarded Book’ describes its preservation from alteration in the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). ‘No one touches it except the purified ones’ may describe that Book or the Qurʾan itself, with the same result: no one has access to the Qurʾan in the guarded Book except the purified. Al-Mizan prefers mass, ‘touching,’ as knowing the Qurʾan in that Book, not merely physical contact. The muṭahharūn are those whom God has cleansed of disobedience, sin, and, at the highest level, every attachment besides Him; this better fits cognitive access than ritual cleanliness. They include righteous angels and purified human beings, including those covered by the thorough purification of the People of the Household (33:33), and the commentary rejects restricting them to angels without proof. It nonetheless allows a secondary legal reading: the wording may be a prohibition, or a declarative statement intended as one, against touching the written Qurʾan without ritual purity; muṭṭahharūn can likewise be read as a contraction of mutaṭahharūn. Al-Zamakhsharī’s physical-contact reading remains possible only if the phrase refers to the Qurʾan’s written text. Tanzīl then describes the Qurʾan as gradually sent down from the Lord of all worlds so people can understand what only the purified could access in the guarded Book; as their Lord, God requires them to believe and heed it.

verses.81: Al-Mizan identifies ‘this discourse’ as the Qurʾan. Idhān, originally softening with oil, figuratively means treating something as unimportant; the rhetorical question rebukes them for taking the Qurʾan lightly.
verses.82: Al-Mizan records that rizq may be their allotted share of goodness from the Qurʾan, which they replace with denial; it may be the Qurʾan itself as spiritual provision; or the verse may imply that they substitute denial for thanks for their provision.
verses.83: Al-Mizan says the challenge returns to the deniers of Qurʾanic teaching about Resurrection and recompense: if they are truthful, they should restore the soul when it reaches a dying person’s throat. The soul’s reaching the throat figures death taking complete hold; the onlookers are powerless while God encompasses the dying person and His angelic emissaries are nearer than they are, though unseen. The repeated challenge emphasizes their incapacity. Madīnīn means subject to recompense, so inability to return the departing soul proves death is God’s decree, bringing souls forth for Resurrection and Final Judgment, not mere chance that they might repel.

verses.88: Al-Mizan returns to the three groups at death and afterward: if the dying person is among the Foremost brought near to God, he receives rūḥ, rest from grief and pain, rayḥān, abundant provision, and a garden of bliss. It records an alternative that rayḥān is paradise-scented basil smelled at death.

verses.90: Al-Mizan says the address shifts from ‘he’ to the dying member of the People of the Right Hand: he is told ‘peace for you.’ The phrase may mean he is singled out for peace and nothing but goodness from his peers and friends, or that they send him greetings of peace; other interpretations are reported.

verses.92: Al-Mizan explains that the impugning, astray deceased receive boiling water and Hell. Their denial is named before their error because obstinate, wilful rejection of truth makes them punishable; those merely astray would be mustaḍʿafīn and would not reach this state. The earlier order, ‘astray deniers’ (56:51), suits its immediate answer to their resurrection-denying question, so it begins with their being astray.

verses.95: Al-Mizan defines ḥaqq as knowledge corresponding to reality and yaqīn as knowledge without ambiguity or doubt. Their expository iḍāfa emphasizes that the preceding account of the three groups is certain, indubitable truth.
verses.96: Al-Mizan says the closing command follows the Qurʾan’s truthfulness and its account of humanity at death, Resurrection, and recompense: invoke and exalt the All-supreme Lord, rejecting the spurious views and arguments of astray deniers.
